title: Graphs of Rates of Change

findings.finding: The worked example uses substitution and solving a one-step equation without rehearsing either substantial prerequisite.
findings.breakdown: Students must distinguish evaluating an expression from finding an unknown input while learning to connect the context, graph and equation.
findings.checked: The preceding topic rehearses calculating and interpreting gradients. Neither its teaching nor the supplied practice rehearses substitution or solving coefficient equations. This topic has no opening review.
findings.assumptions: These algebraic methods are prior knowledge, consistent with the course library. Calculator availability does not affect the finding.

repair.proposal: Before p5-example, add: (a) If y=6x, find y when x=4. (b) If C=1.5N, find C when N=8. (c) Solve 8t=56. (d) Solve 1.5N=18. Answers: 24, 12, 7, 12. Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: Students rehearse both substitution and solving a coefficient equation before the example.

findings.finding: The car's journey total establishes an average speed, but does not establish the constant speed required for the requested graph and predictions.
findings.breakdown: Students are asked to infer a straight distance–time graph and d=25t from one journey total, risking the rule that any such total determines constant speed.
findings.checked: Earlier tasks supply either a straight graph, a direct-variation equation or an explicit constant-rate condition. None supplies that condition for this journey.
findings.assumptions: The intended model is direct variation, as confirmed by the requested rule and predictions.

repair.proposal: Change the stem to: “A solar-powered car travels at a constant speed, covering 100 km in 4 hours.”

findings.doneWhen: The stem supplies the condition justifying the straight graph and predictions.

findings.finding: Extend the bike journey by comparing journeys at twice the original speed.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up connects doubling speed with doubling distance over a fixed time and halving time over a fixed distance.
findings.checked: The original speed is 10 km/h. At 20 km/h, 3.5 hours gives 70 km and 55 km takes 2.75 hours. All calculations use methods already demonstrated.
findings.assumptions: Both riders travel at constant speeds.

repair.proposal: After p9-q5-d, add optional parts: (e) A second rider travels at 20 km/h. How far does this rider travel in 3.5 hours? Answer: 70 km. (f) How long does this rider take to travel 55 km? Answer: 2.75 hours. (g) Compared with part d(i), how has doubling the speed changed the distance travelled in 3.5 hours? Answer: the distance doubled. (h) Compared with part d(ii), how has doubling the speed changed the time needed to travel 55 km? Answer: the time halved.

findings.doneWhen: The optional follow-up uses the original journey's values to compare both effects of doubling speed.

findings.finding: In the supplied order, students must derive a combined exchange equation from two graphs before attempting the available numerical two-stage conversion.
findings.breakdown: p16-q7 introduces choosing an intermediate currency, extracting two rates and combining them into a new equation together after single-relationship conversions.
findings.checked: p14-q1 through p15-q5 use one conversion relationship at a time. p16-q6-b provides a smaller step: converting a specified amount through AUD using the equation from part a and another supplied equation.
findings.assumptions: The supplied practice order is the teaching order. Calculator availability does not affect the transition.

repair.proposal: Place p16-q6 before p16-q7, retaining both questions and all their parts.

findings.doneWhen: Students complete the numerical two-stage conversion before deriving a combined exchange equation.

findings.finding: Quantify the effect of the changed euro conversion rate on Sandy's spending money.
findings.breakdown: This gives a numerical consequence of the gradient change considered in the existing part b.
findings.checked: US$150 converts to A$200, giving A$800 altogether. The new rate gives €520, which is €40 more than the original €480. The equation and conversions use established direct-variation methods.
findings.assumptions: The US dollar conversion rate remains unchanged.

repair.proposal: After p17-q8-b, add optional parts: (c) The US dollar conversion rate stays the same, but A$100 now buys €65. Write the new equation relating euros E to Australian dollars A. Answer: E=0.65A. (d) How many euros would Sandy now receive for all her money in part a? Answer: €520. (e) How many more euros is this than before? Answer: €40.

findings.doneWhen: The follow-up connects the steeper conversion line with Sandy receiving more euros.

findings.finding: Extend the factory model to expose its constant total production cost.
findings.breakdown: Multiplying unit cost by the number of boxes gives a concrete interpretation of the inverse-variation constant.
findings.checked: The given values imply c=256/n. For 256 boxes the unit cost is $1; total costs for both 256 and 128 boxes are $256. Multiplication and substitution suffice.
findings.assumptions: Box counts are positive integers and total production cost is modelled as unit cost multiplied by quantity.

repair.proposal: After the existing equation-and-sketch task add optional parts: (a) What is the cost per box when 256 boxes are produced? Answer: $1. (b) What is the total cost of producing those 256 boxes? Answer: $256. (c) What is the total cost when 128 boxes are produced? Answer: $256. (d) Why are these two total costs equal in this model? Answer: Multiplying the cost per box, 256/n, by n gives $256 in each case.

findings.doneWhen: The numerical follow-up exposes the fixed product in the existing model.

findings.finding: The teaching equates gradient with speed without explaining the change needed when distance from home decreases.
findings.breakdown: On returning journeys the gradient is negative, while speed is positive. Students need gradient magnitude to distinguish slowing down from speeding up on falling curves.
findings.checked: p27 models speed only with rising graphs. Its falling-curve illustrations and p28-q1 describe changes in distance rather than explicitly connecting negative gradients with speed. The explanations accompanying p29 answers supply this connection only after the classifications are requested.
findings.assumptions: The p29 graphs represent journeys with distance measured from home, as their shared stem states. Calculator use is irrelevant.

repair.proposal: Before the p29 classifications add: “Here, distance is measured from home and decreases when someone travels towards home. Speed is the steepness of the graph, ignoring whether it slopes up or down. A downward curve that becomes steeper shows increasing speed; one that flattens shows decreasing speed.”

findings.doneWhen: Students are explicitly shown how speed relates to negative gradients before classifying returning journeys.

findings.finding: The topic does not rehearse signed endpoint differences or the rectangle, triangle and composite-area calculations used in its examples.
findings.breakdown: Following the examples requires recalling subtraction order and area formulas while learning the new interpretations of gradient and area.
findings.checked: Earlier teaching includes endpoint differences, but the immediately preceding topic concerns qualitative graphs of filling containers. It does not rehearse these algebraic or area calculations. The speed–time topic combines them and has no opening review.
findings.assumptions: Signed differences and elementary area formulas are prior knowledge. Calculator availability does not remove these decisions.

repair.proposal: Add four short opening items: (a) A quantity falls from 16 to 0 while time increases from 14 to 16. Find the change in the quantity and the elapsed time. Answers: −16 and 2. (b) Find the area of a rectangle with base 30 cm and height 20 cm. Answer: 600 cm². (c) Find the area of a triangle with base 20 cm and perpendicular height 10 cm. Answer: 100 cm². (d) A shape consists of a 4 cm by 6 cm rectangle and two adjoining triangles with bases 4 cm and 12 cm, each with perpendicular height 6 cm. Find its total area. Answer: 72 cm². Keep the complete review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: The teacher can check signed changes and the required area calculations before the worked examples.

findings.finding: The example uses an unknown in a denominator without rehearsing that prior algebraic skill.
findings.breakdown: The transition from 95=400/t to t=400/95 requires a rearrangement that the preceding coefficient-equation practice does not rehearse.
findings.checked: Earlier direct-variation and conversion teaching solves equations with a multiplied unknown. The immediately preceding conversion topic does not rehearse an unknown denominator, and this topic has no review.
findings.assumptions: Rearranging these equations is prior knowledge, consistent with the course library. A calculator does not supply the rearrangement.

repair.proposal: Before p18-inverse-definition, add: (a) Solve 6=42/x. (b) Solve 15=120/t. (c) Solve 25=90/u. Answers: x=7, t=8, u=3.6. Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: Students rehearse isolating an unknown denominator before p18-example-time.

findings.finding: Extend the cylindrical-container context by changing the pouring rate partway through filling.
findings.breakdown: Students connect a doubled pouring rate in a cylinder with a doubled height–time gradient.
findings.checked: The cylinder has constant cross-section. Four minutes at 3 cm/min gives 12 cm; two further minutes at 6 cm/min gives a final depth of 24 cm. The graph uses previously taught constant rates and straight segments.
findings.assumptions: The container starts empty and does not overflow.

repair.proposal: After p36-q1-e, add optional parts: (f) In container a, water initially rises by 3 cm each minute. How deep is it after 4 minutes, starting empty? Answer: 12 cm. (g) The pouring rate then doubles for the next 2 minutes. What is the final depth, assuming the container does not overflow? Answer: 24 cm. (h) Sketch the height–time graph for these 6 minutes. Answer: straight segments joining (0,0), (4,12) and (6,24), with time in minutes horizontally and height in centimetres vertically.

findings.doneWhen: The optional follow-up connects the changed pouring rate to two distinct constant gradients.

findings.finding: The example substitutes −16 and 2 without explicitly obtaining those changes from the endpoints.
findings.breakdown: The graph supplies speed and time coordinates, whereas the calculation requires signed change in speed and elapsed time. The connecting calculations are omitted.
findings.checked: The acceleration is correctly (0−16)/(16−14)=−8 m/s². Earlier gradient work and the following guided practice establish endpoint subtraction, but this example still substitutes derived quantities without showing their origins.
findings.assumptions: Students know rise over run. Calculator availability is immaterial.

repair.proposal: Before the calculation, add: 'Change in speed = 0−16 = −16 m/s; elapsed time = 16−14 = 2 s.'

findings.doneWhen: Both substituted changes are explicitly connected to the graph's endpoint coordinates.

findings.finding: Vary initial speed while holding elapsed time and speed increase constant.
findings.breakdown: The sequence isolates why acceleration depends on the change in speed rather than the final speed.
findings.checked: The three rising segments each have acceleration 2 m/s²; the final falling segment has acceleration −2 m/s². Endpoint subtraction and negative acceleration are taught before this exercise.
findings.assumptions: Use the same axis scales for the three comparison graphs.

repair.proposal: Append graph parts g–j under p43-q1's existing instruction. Add only: 'Predict before calculating.' Draw straight speed–time segments: (g) (0,0) to (3,6); (h) (0,4) to (3,10); (i) (0,12) to (3,18); (j) (0,11) to (4,3), with seconds horizontally and m/s vertically. Answers: 2, 2, 2 and −2 m/s². Parts g–i vary initial speed while keeping elapsed time and speed increase fixed; j is the unpatterned follow-up.

findings.doneWhen: Students compare the three equal accelerations before attempting the falling-speed follow-up.

protectedGroups.observation: Rate units follow the order of the axes: fuel per distance and distance per fuel describe different rates.
protectedGroups.varies: Which quantity occupies each axis and whether a numerical calculation is requested.
protectedGroups.invariant: The fuel–distance context and the interpretation of gradient as vertical quantity per horizontal quantity.

protectedGroups.observation: Speed is consistently distance divided by time, expressed in the units supplied by each graph.
protectedGroups.varies: Endpoint values, distance units, time units and whether division gives an integer.
protectedGroups.invariant: A straight distance–time segment from the origin with a labelled endpoint.

protectedGroups.observation: An equation provides an exact model result where reading the graph gives an estimate.
protectedGroups.varies: The representation and precision of the solution method.
protectedGroups.invariant: The conversion relationship and the requested conversion of 30 litres.

protectedGroups.observation: The same forward and reverse conversion decisions work with a less convenient conversion constant.
protectedGroups.varies: The context, constant and arithmetic precision.
protectedGroups.invariant: The two-row table structure with two forward and two reverse conversions.

protectedGroups.observation: For the same delivery duration and target volume, a higher flow rate gives more water and a shorter delivery time.
protectedGroups.varies: The volume reached after five minutes, hence the flow rate.
protectedGroups.invariant: Water-flow context, time-axis units, 30-minute delivery period and 1000-litre target.

protectedGroups.observation: Increasing the workforce decreases completion time for the same job; doubling from three to six people halves the time.
protectedGroups.invariant: The job and the product nt=6.

protectedGroups.observation: Different base–height pairs preserve the same area, culminating in the product equation.
protectedGroups.varies: Given dimension and direction of graph reading.

protectedGroups.observation: A constant rate can increase or decrease a quantity.
Direction of change and increasing or decreasing steepness are separate decisions.
protectedGroups.varies: Rising versus falling and steepening versus flattening.

protectedGroups.observation: Changes over equal time intervals connect numerical readings with qualitative rate descriptions and steepness.
protectedGroups.invariant: The four supplied journeys and one-second interval length.

protectedGroups.observation: The same journey distinguishes positive, zero and negative acceleration through the gradient.
protectedGroups.varies: The direction and steepness of the speed-time segment.
protectedGroups.invariant: The context, axes and interpretation of gradient as acceleration.

protectedGroups.observation: Students apply the same calculation to speeding up, constant speed and slowing down.
protectedGroups.varies: The speed change and interval duration.
protectedGroups.invariant: The graph, context and acceleration method.

protectedGroups.observation: Reusing the animal graphs deliberately connects gradient calculations with area calculations.
protectedGroups.varies: The quantity sought: acceleration first, then distance and separation.
protectedGroups.invariant: The chase context and both speed traces.

The attached images end at page 34. Page 35 graph and circuit specifications support a reading of the intended tasks, but the actual axis labels and circuit features cannot be independently inspected; no finding is based on those unseen drawing details.

sequences.title: Rate from a direct variation model

dropped.reason: The proposed interval totals largely repeat the distance-change calculations already required in p30-q1-i–iv, while the final-reading comparison chiefly tests the tangential distinction between a reference-point reading and distance travelled. It is weaker than the four retained extensions.

candidates.finding: Compare total distance travelled with the final distance reading for returning cars.

dropped.reason: The supplied p42 diagram descriptions omit the numerical dimensions and annotations needed to establish that their origins are unshown, so the first-example allegation cannot be verified. For the second example, p41-guided already identifies and calculates the same four-second and twelve-second intervals, defeating the claim that these widths arrive without preceding support.

candidates.finding: The area working substitutes interval widths and a triangle height without showing how they are obtained from the graph's endpoint values.

dropped.reason: The mathematics is correct: the comparison car takes 40 seconds, saves 20 seconds and is 1200 m farther after 40 seconds. However, retain at most four suggestions; the four retained extensions more directly expose their topics' central relationships, whereas these parts principally add further time and distance calculations.

candidates.finding: Compare the journey with covering the same distance at the final speed throughout.
